title: More Testosterone Won’t Make a Better Soldier or a Tougher Man – Aggression and Strength Drive T Levels, Not the Other Way Around
gist: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's July 2026 order that US service members aged 30 and older be tested annually for testosterone never defines what counts as 'low,' a threshold that varies by lab and guideline. Psychologist Adam Stanaland argues the causal arrow runs backward — aggression and strength raise testosterone rather than the reverse — and lands the policy amid a prescription boom to nearly 12 million in 2025, up 154 percent since 2020, driven largely by online lifestyle clinics.

insights.claim: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in July 2026 that United States service members aged 30 and older will have their testosterone tested every year.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: A federal employer mandating annual hormone screening creates a large captive testing and treatment funnel — watch lab-services and TRT prescribing volumes.
insights.quote: United States service members ages 30 and older will have their testosterone tested every year
insights.locator: When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced

insights.claim: Neither Hegseth nor the Pentagon specified what testosterone level would count as low enough to require treatment, an omission that matters because where 'low' begins depends on the lab running the test and the guidelines the doctor follows.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: An undefined clinical threshold makes the size of the treated population a policy variable rather than a medical fact — the eventual cutoff decides how big the market is.
insights.quote: neither he nor the Pentagon specified what level of the hormone would be considered “low” enough to require treatment—a telling omission
insights.locator: When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced

insights.claim: The military lifestyle itself is more likely to lower testosterone levels than to raise them, making a screening mandate aimed at service members self-undermining.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: If service conditions suppress the hormone being screened for, mass testing converts an occupational stressor into a diagnosis and a prescription rather than a fix.
insights.quote: Ironically, the military lifestyle itself is more likely to lower T levels.
insights.locator: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is requiring service members to screen

insights.claim: US testosterone prescriptions climbed to nearly 12 million in 2025, up 154 percent since 2020, with the fastest growth among men in their late 30s and 40s.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: A 154 percent five-year expansion in a single hormone category is a live growth market — and a live target for reimbursement or regulatory pushback.
insights.quote: Prescriptions have climbed to nearly 12 million in 2025, up 154 percent since 2020, and fastest among men in their late 30s and 40s.
insights.locator: The announcement lands amid a national testosterone craze

insights.claim: Online clinics selling testosterone as a lifestyle upgrade have largely driven the recent rise in prescriptions.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: Direct-to-consumer telehealth, not traditional endocrinology, is the demand channel — the growth is distribution-led and therefore vulnerable to prescribing-rule changes.
insights.quote: Online clinics that sell testosterone as a lifestyle upgrade have largely driven this rise in prescriptions.
insights.locator: The announcement lands amid a national testosterone craze

themes.theme: Reversed causality on hormones and toughness

insights.claim: The intuitive belief that more testosterone makes a man tougher and more fit to fight is mostly wrong; aggression and physical strength drive testosterone levels rather than the other way around.
insights.speaker: Adam Stanaland
insights.so_what: If the causal arrow is reversed, supplementation cannot deliver the trait buyers and policymakers are paying for — the entire lifestyle-TRT value proposition rests on a misread.
insights.quote: while the idea that more testosterone makes a man tougher and more fit to fight seems intuitive, it’s also mostly wrong
insights.locator: As a psychologist who studies masculinity
